items.title: Surging jobsite raids put 370,000 new home completions at risk
items.description: America’s homebuilders entered the fall with 256,000 newly constructed homes still under construction for sale and another 114,000 permitted or otherwise classified as not yet started. Together, those 370,000 homes represent an enormous amount of work builders still have to complete, along with intensifying business risk tied to their ability to do so. The figures come from the Census Bureau’s August New Home Sales report, as highlighted by housing economist Bill McBride of Calculated Risk . They take on added urgency as builders enter the final months of 2026, racing to move homes through the remaining stages of construction, complete deliveries before winter and year-end, and convert invested capital back into cash. These are homes for sale, not homes already under contract. But that distinction should not be mistaken for a lack of financial exposure. By the time a builder has secured land, developed lots, obtained permits, and committed to a speculative home, the builder has already invested capital and assumed risk. For the 256,000 homes under construction, those commitments are substantially further along. Many of those homes are approaching the point where a reliable sequence of finishing trades determines whether a project closes on schedule or slips into another month, quarter, or year. Drywall installers, painters, flooring crews, finish carpenters, and other subcontractors must arrive in the right order, with little room for delays. That’s where a serious problem has taken hold in the homebuilding landscape. Just as homebuilders need to complete work already underway, the skilled trade crews required to finish those homes are becoming harder to secure. Immigration enforcement is adding another layer of disruption to an already constrained workforce , threatening construction schedules, increasing carrying costs and putting additional pressure on businesses whose margins and cash flows are already stretched. It would be one thing if immigration enforcement were merely reducing the availability of construction workers. What’s now becoming clear is that an industry already struggling to sell homes may be unable to reliably finish the homes it has invested so much upfront capital in. A labor shortage in a slowing housing market Normally, slower homebuilding activity would ease competition for construction workers. With fewer new starts, builders should have more flexibility to secure the crews needed to complete projects already underway. But residential construction does not operate in isolation. Skilled workers and subcontractors can pursue opportunities in commercial construction, infrastructure, and the rapidly expanding data-center sector , where demand for certain trades remains strong. As a result, a slowdown in new-home production does not necessarily translate into greater labor availability for homebuilders. Immigration enforcement is now ratcheting up that squeeze. The combination is particularly dangerous at this point in the construction and business cycle. Builders are entering the final weeks of the year with significant capital tied up in homes at various stages of completion. Many are trying to complete projects before winter weather complicates schedules and before year-end financial and delivery targets come due. A shortage of framing crews can delay a project early in its timeline. A shortage of drywall installers, painters, flooring specialists, or finish carpenters can prevent a nearly completed home from being delivered, even after most of its construction costs have already been incurred. A home that is 90% complete is not 90% of a closing. Until the remaining work is finished, inspections are passed and a buyer can take possession, the builder may be unable to realize the expected sales proceeds. items.title: Mortgage Rates Hold Steady as 10-yr Treasury Yields Stabilize
items.description: Data , Economic Coverage , Housing Finance , Weekly Mortgage Rate Mortgage Rates Hold Steady as 10-yr Treasury Yields Stabilize By Jiayi Xu Oct 15, 2026 What happened to mortgage rates this week? The Freddie Mac 30-year mortgage rate held steady at 7.4% this week as the 10-year Treasury yield stabilized around 5.2%. September’s CPI came in slightly hotter than expected, and of rising concern is the uptick in core CPI, which suggests that price pressures may be broadening beyond energy into other categories. Looking ahead, the acceleration in core CPI, a sign of sticky inflation, reinforces the case for another rate hike by December and could set the stage for additional hikes in early 2027. In other words, mortgage rates are unlikely to ease anytime soon, but bringing inflation under control would pave the way for lower rates and a much-needed boost to affordability for the year ahead. What does this mean for the housing market? With mortgage rates holding above 7%, many prospective buyers have pulled back, and Realtor.com pending home sales dropped substantially in September as elevated rates continue to weigh on demand. Yet sitting on the sidelines isn’t the only option. Buyers who stay engaged may find footing in a market where motivated sellers are increasingly willing to negotiate. The share of price cuts hit a four-year high in September, and the share of listings pulled from the market remained in line with a year ago , suggesting sellers are committed to transacting. For home buyers, it is important to rate-proof their budget and ensure they are financially positioned to act when the right opportunity arises.

items.title: Lenders Accuse Nord Group Entities Of Pocketing Rents, Faking Insurance As Multifamily Empire Crumbles
items.description: Lenders Accuse Nord Group Entities Of Pocketing Rents, Faking Insurance As Multifamily Empire Crumbles October 15, 2026 | 6:59 pm ET Maddy McCarty, Houston Magistrate Judge Andrew Edison had run out of patience. He had just heard arguments from attorneys for Freddie Mac , which had foreclosed on a 228-unit apartment complex in Lake Jackson, Texas, claiming that the property's previous owner was still collecting rents. The owner, a subsidiary of New York-based Nord Group , had stopped making mortgage payments 18 months earlier. But it nevertheless sued its lender over alleged breach of contract, eventually claiming that it still legally possessed the property after foreclosure due to a technicality. Edison wasn’t amused, calling the behavior “pretty damn egregious.” “I mean, come on,” Edison said during a May 26 hearing. “The property has been foreclosed. Get out of the damn property. Stop taking money that doesn't belong to you.” A fed-up federal judge is just one of a host of issues piling up for Nord Group and its 27-year-old CEO and co-founder, Saqif Noor. Instagram/Saqif Noor Saqif Noor in an Instagram post shared Oct. 22, 2023 Lenders and investors have accused Nord entities of stealing rents, providing fake insurance records and keeping buildings in an “alarming state of neglect that poses serious health, safety and habitability concerns.” Court filings detail hazards including sewage backups, mold, vermin and cat feces rendering apartments unlivable. Nord Group is one of many investors that spent heavily on apartments in the ultralow-interest-rate environment of 2021 and 2022, but its collapse stands out for the apparent deception behind its buying spree and the rapid deterioration of its properties. Investigators are circling, and Nord's 11-property portfolio built between 2021 and 2023, fueled by nearly $400M in largely government-backed debt, is slipping out of its grasp. In phone calls in February and April with an investor, recordings of which were shared with Bisnow , Noor said he signed for his father on loan documents, that the FBI has questioned his former partner, and that he’s pretty sure he will spend time behind bars. “I think camp time is inevitable. It’s inevitable. It’s going to happen,” Noor said on the call. “Prison time. Camp sounds a little nicer.” In an email to Bisnow , Noor denied these conversations took place. His former partner, Baruch Teitelbaum, denied being questioned by the FBI. When presented with a detailed list of questions, Noor wrote, “A lot of the info here on your email seem to be baseless false,” and referred comment on Nord litigation to his attorney. Noor didn't respond to follow-up questions. Nord Group and its subsidiaries have been party to at least two dozen lawsuits, bankruptcy cases and appeals since late 2023, according to hundreds of pages of court records reviewed by Bisnow . Numerous cases have been dismissed or halted by bankruptcy proceedings, but at least five remain open, including litigation with Freddie Mac and Fannie Mae and lawsuits from residents who allege negligence resulting in the drowning of a child and a man being shot. A Nord entity denied responsibility in the drowning case. Nord Group never responded in the shooting case, filed last October, and this week was ordered to pay a $6.6M default judgment to the alleged victim. “The Nord Group provides housing for thousands of working-class Americans and is proud of their role in the communities they serve,” Nord's attorney, Jason Kraus, said in a statement. “We cannot comment on any pending court cases and will not litigate through the media, but please understand that mere allegations in lawsuits are just that — allegations specifically drafted to inflame, gain media attention and are not proven facts. The Nord Group of companies vigorously denies all allegations and will continue to defend itself in court.” Noor started Nord Group with backing from his father, Dr. Khaled Noor, and in partnership with Teitel
items.selector_reason: 贷款方指控Nord Group关联实体挪用租金和伪造保险，且其多户住宅帝国正在崩溃。案件涉及公寓资产运营、贷款安全和多户住宅信用风险，行业警示意义较强。

items.title: Build-to-rent communities now eligible for FHA financing
items.description: Politics and policy Build-to-rent communities now eligible for FHA financing By Brad Finkelstein CloseText About Brad twitter nmnbrad mailto bradley.finkelstein@arizent.com linkedin brad-finkelstein-8b2b9a5/ Published October 15, 2026, 4:56 p.m. EDT 3 Min Read Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Processing Content What's at Stake: Whether the new FHA financing will actually lower rents or expand housing supply. Expert Quote: "It does not alter real-world bottlenecks" — Thom Malone, principal economist, Cotality Supporting Data: Fewer than 100,000 annual starts for one specific property type. Overview bullets generated by AI with editorial review. Build-to-rent lending, a property type exempted from the ownership restrictions in the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, got a boost from the Department of Housing and Urban Development on Wednesday. If anything, the Act was expected to create a shift among business-purpose lenders away from single-family rental transactions towards BTR properties. Some BPL originators acquire their production through the correspondent channel. These properties are now eligible for Federal Housing Administration-insurance under two multifamily programs: Section 221(d)(4) for new construction and Section 223(f) for acquisition or refinancing of recently developed rental communities. "In theory, this announcement will lower the cost of capital for BTR by providing more stable and cheaper financing options," said Thom Malone, principal economist for Cotality. "This would increase the supply of rental housing, which would put downward pressure on rents, but that would be blunted since it would also increase demand by making more families choose renting over buying." However, Malone thinks the effects would be extremely small, possibly not even detectable in practice. "Even if the cost of capital is lower, it does not alter real-world bottlenecks like processing delays and restrictive local zoning," Malone continued. BTR is not a large part of the market, he said, with the number of starts totalling fewer than 100,000 a year. "Even if this program increased that by 20%, that would still mean only 15,000 to 20,000 more rental units — a drop in the bucket of the U.S. rental market," Malone said. Still, this change not only helps those who need this type of financing but also gives lenders another product they can offer at a time when industry economists are expecting owner-occupied residential volume to decline 5% in 2027. HUD Secretary Scott Turner. Photographer: Kent Nishimura/Bloomberg Kent Nishimura/Bloomberg "America needs more affordable housing," HUD Secretary Scott Turner said in a press release. "We're eliminating barriers to spur development, expand rental options and improve housing affordability for hardworking American families." While a fair amount of investor-property loans goes through the non-agency market, certain non-owner occupied premises are eligible for government-sponsored enterprise financing. The Community Home Lenders of America, whose membership consists of single-family originators who concentrate on the owner-occupied segment, still sees this announcement as having a broader impact on housing. "We need an 'all hands on deck' approach to our nation's affordable housing challenges," Scott Olson, the group's executive director, said. "So while this does not directly affect homeownership — CHLA's top priority as the trade group exclusively representing non-bank single-family lenders — housing is a continuum, and this is a very constructive action, which CHLA supports, to develop more affordable rental housing." Build-to-rent communities typically consist of single-family homes, duplexes or triplexes. Under the change, FHA insurance will cover both site-built and manufactured home BTRs and treat them under the same terms and conditions as traditional multifamily rental developments. items.title: Brookfield Veteran Departs To Become Pretium's Global Real Estate Lead
items.description: Brookfield Veteran Departs To Become Pretium's Global Real Estate Lead October 15, 2026 | 7:07 pm ET Ciara Long, New York City A longtime Brookfield exec is headed to Pretium Partners to oversee the alternative investment manager’s real estate debt and equity business. Unsplash/Yasar Qureshi Christopher Reilly is swapping his seat at Brookfield Asset Management , where he has spent the last 14 years, for the role at Pretium, PERE News reported , citing multiple anonymous sources. Brookfield declined to comment, while Pretium did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Reilly arrives at residential-focused Pretium as it launches its seventh U.S. opportunistic single-family rental fund. In 2020, he was tapped to oversee Brookfield's real estate solutions group when the firm created the department designed to focus on recapitalizations and secondaries. Two years later, he spearheaded the launch of Brookfield's first dedicated real estate secondaries fund, which closed in 2024 with $1.3B in commitments. Brookfield launched a follow-up vehicle in October 2025, this time targeting $2B in fundraising. Prior to his tenure at the solutions group, Reilly was Brookfield Real Estate Funds’ head of originations. He’s now stepping in to fill the shoes of Josh Pristaw, who left Pretium to take up the mantle as Clarion Partners ’ managing director and president last year. New York-based Pretium has around $70B of assets under management, according to its website, and closed its sixth opportunistic single-family rental fund at $1.3B in 2024, according to PERE. It manages roughly $32B in real estate equity and $6B in real estate debt, as well as a $29B residential mortgage platform, according to PERE. Reilly isn't the only recent departure from Brookfield's real estate solutions group: Marcus Day, previously a managing director of U.S. and Asia-Pacific investment strategy, was announced this week as head of LaSalle Global Solutions at JLL subsidiary LaSalle Investment Management. Alison Giampa will take over managing Brookfield Real Estate Solutions’ portfolio, while Kayley Laren will run U.S. investment strategy and Alexis Prevot will take on the APAC region in addition to Europe, PERE reports. Pretium has made two other high-profile hires this year. In March , the firm hired Joel Sulkes as its managing director of insurance risk management, followed one month later by the hire of Graham Dorland as managing director of business development for capital raising, business and product development. items.title: 3 notable office-to-residential conversions in DC
items.description: An article from 3 notable office-to-residential conversions in DC For a conversion project to be successful, “You need the good fundamentals. You need a good location,” National Real Estate Development’s Peter Epstein told Multifamily Dive. Published Oct. 15, 2026 Julie Strupp Senior Editor Share Copy link Email LinkedIn X/Twitter Facebook Print License Add us on Google Aviator House, an office-to-residential conversion, just opened its doors in the Dupont Circle neighborhood in the District of Columbia. Julie Strupp/Multifamily Dive Listen to the article 7 min This audio is auto-generated. Please let us know if you have feedback . Faced with an excess of underused office buildings downtown along with a persisting housing shortage, Washington, D.C., is becoming a leader in office-to-residential conversions. Nationwide, the number of conversion projects jumped 28% year over year at the beginning of 2026, Smart Cities Dive reported. RentCafe data showed that New York City far outpaced other jurisdictions, with 16,358 conversion units in progress, while D.C. ranked second with 8,479 such units underway. With office demand sapped by the pandemic, D.C. Mayor Muriel Bowser has focused on residential conversions to incentivize development and draw people to live downtown. In 2024, D.C. launched the Housing in Downtown initiative , offering a 20-year tax break and other incentives to catalyze commercial-to-residential conversions, per the program website. Last October, the city expanded HID’s eligibility area, “greatly increasing the pool for potential conversion projects in the District.” On Wednesday, Multifamily Dive witnessed Aviator House officially open its doors — the first HID-supported project to do so. Read on to learn more about the district’s newest conversion and two others on the way. Aviator House, Dupont Circle Aviator House’s entryway. Courtesy of National Real Estate Development Aviator House, redesigned to honor its former use as the headquarters of the Air Line Pilots Association, has been transformed into 157 studio, one- and two-bedroom apartments, per a press release shared with Multifamily Dive. D.C.-based National Real Estate Advisors owns the eight-story, 1972-vintage building and developed the project through its subsidiary, National Real Estate Development. Peter Epstein, managing director of development at National Real Estate Development and project lead, told Multifamily Dive that the firm decided to convert the building because it was “maybe 50% leased” in the wake of the pandemic. One of the first challenges was making the layout work for apartments. “Every conversion project is such a puzzle. Financially, the project has to make sense, but physically, the building has to be able to convert,” Epstein said. “We felt that by being clever with how we laid out the floor plate, we could get units that were pretty efficient and sort of minimize the super deep units that you can get sometimes in office conversions.” The project broke ground in October 2024, with Clark Construction as the general contractor and ECA as the architect, per the release. The firm leaned into design to differentiate it from other apartment complexes, according to Epstein: “We wanted it to have an actual identity and something that people would viscerally respond to and be drawn to.” A living room at Aviator House. items.title: Hospital Construction Costs Are Climbing. Atlanta's Healthcare Systems Keep Building
items.description: Hospital Construction Costs Are Climbing. Atlanta's Healthcare Systems Keep Building October 15, 2026 | 6:25 pm ET Jarred Schenke, Atlanta Hospital systems in Atlanta are expanding their real estate to reach more patients, even as rising construction costs and elevated interest rates make financing more difficult. Piedmont Healthcare last month said it plans to invest nearly $600M to build a new relocation hospital in the metro area, a project that would be the healthcare giant’s second-largest capital outlay in its history. In August, Atrium Health , along with Morehouse School of Medicine, got approval for a $700M teaching hospital and care network designed to serve Central and South Fulton County communities. “Our goal is to be at everybody’s front door,” Keishia Niblack, director of real estate at Piedmont Healthcare, said at Bisnow ’s Atlanta Healthcare Conference this week. “Our goal is to focus a lot on making sure that our community can stay in their community, and they don't have to drive an hour or two to get to actual top-quality care.” Bisnow/Jarred Schenke Remedy Medical Properties' David Martin, Anchor Health Properties' Mervyn Alphonso, Evergreen Medical Properties' Justin Carpenter and JE Dunn Construction's Carla Bowron She said she expects Piedmont and other healthcare systems to focus on hyperlocalized outpatient and medical centers within 5 miles of residential communities in Metro Atlanta. The growing aging population in the U.S. is forcing healthcare systems to rely more heavily on outpatient care, driving a need to build more facilities, panelists said at The Carlyle. Healthcare systems generally spend less per patient for care at outpatient facilities than in-hospital stays. But health systems are having to navigate spiking debt and construction costs as well as cuts to federal reimbursements . Hospital systems are also tallying lower profit margins as operating costs rise over the past year, according to data from Strata Decision Technology . Operating margins were 1% to 1.5% in the second half of last year but turned negative in the first quarter of 2026. They turned positive in March, according to Strata, reaching 0.7% by June. New medical office building deliveries are expected to drop 26% in 2026, to the lowest level in more than a decade, according to CBRE . But spending on hospital and clinic construction is expected to jump 11.6% to $30.7B this year compared to 2025, the Healthcare Financial Management Association reports. The cost to develop hospitals and medical facilities averaged a little more than $370 per SF in 2020, according to the RS Means Data construction costs estimator . By 2026, costs ranged from $439 to nearly $455 per SF, according to RS Means . Costs are making it difficult for developers to find medical operators willing to pay the rents needed to justify new construction, said David Martin , executive vice president of Remedy Medical Properties . “It’s a tough, tough environment to deliver a new medical office building today,” Martin said, adding that the delta between existing medical office rents nationally and rents needed to fill newly delivered space is nearly $10 per SF. New technology is also pushing up infrastructure costs for medical offices and hospitals, including dynamic wayfinding signage, McCarthy Building Cos . Project Director Kyle Orr said. That’s making it harder for healthcare systems to draw a profit on new developments. “Just because you build a brand-new medical office building in the fastest-growing submarket of Atlanta, it doesn't guarantee a profitable venture,” Martin said. items.title: Beazer Homes stockholders approve $2.2B sale to Dream Finders
items.description: The stockholders of Beazer Homes overwhelmingly approved the Dream Finders Homes ’ pending acquisition of Beazer at a special meeting held earlier this week, moving the deal closer to closing, the companies announced on Thursday. The stockholder vote is one of the final remaining conditions for the transaction. The parties previously received early termination of the waiting period under the Hart-Scott-Rodino Antitrust Improvements Act, and Dream Finders said it expects to complete the deal on Oct. 20, 2026, using previously disclosed available or committed financing sources. Under the terms of the all-cash transaction. first announced in August, Dream Finders will acquire Beazer at an enterprise value of approximately $2.2 billion. Beazer shareholders will receive $33.50 in cash for each share of Beazer common stock, implying a purchase price-to-book value multiple of 0.8x. Beazer is a national homebuilder operating in 15 markets across 13 states. Once the acquisition closes, Dream Finders and Beazer are expected to form what the companies describe as the nation’s sixth-largest homebuilder by volume, with complementary geographic footprints and expanded product offerings. The combined platform will operate in 26 markets and approximately 520 active communities across the Southeast, Mid-Atlantic, Texas, the West and the Midwest mdash; regions that include many of the country’s highest-demand housing corridors. This larger footprint will increase the company’s reach across both entry-level and move-up communities, positioning the combined builder to serve a broader buyer base across multiple price points. They also expect to realize purchasing efficiencies and operational scale that could support more competitive pricing and a more streamlined homebuying experience.
